column2: NHTSA's Final Environmental Impact Statement establishes an Average Fuel Economy Standard (AFES) for model year 1979 nonpassenger automobiles (pickup trucks, vans, and jeep-type four-wheel drive vehicles) rated at 6,000 pounds GVWR or less, setting 17.2 mpg for most NPAs and a separate 15.8 mpg standard for jeep-type four-wheel drive vehicles. The action affects domestic manufacturers (GM, Ford, Chrysler, AMC, International Harvester) and addresses the fact that motor vehicles under 10,000 lbs GVWR accounted for 38 percent of national petroleum consumption in 1975. NHTSA considered alternatives including taking no action, extending the standard to vehicles above 6,000 lbs GVWR, extending it to model years beyond 1979, and setting higher or lower standards. The standard is expected to save 69.1–102.7 million gallons of gasoline annually with minor adverse impacts including increased use of aluminum, plastics, and platinum/palladium for catalytic converters. All major manufacturers submitted comments disputing NHTSA's assumptions about achievable fuel economy and emissions penalties, leading the agency to lower the proposed 18.7 mpg standard to 17.2 mpg and create a separate class for jeep-type vehicles.

column2: Four basic alternatives were considered: take no action, extend the scope of the standard to NPAs above 6,000 pounds GVWR, make the standard effective for years beyond MY 1979, and set a higher or lower standard. Taking no action was rejected because Title V requires the Secretary to prescribe standards; extending coverage above 6,000 lbs GVWR was rejected because baseline data were unavailable; and higher/lower standards were rejected because higher levels could induce market shifts and lower levels would fail the 'maximum feasible' requirement. The final rule also adopted two classes—jeep-type vehicles at 15.8 mpg and all other NPAs at 17.2 mpg—lowering the proposed 18.7 mpg level by 8 percent to account for the revised testing procedure.

column2: Beneficial impacts include annual gasoline savings of 69.1–102.7 million gallons (691–1027 million gallons over the fleet lifetime), with net energy savings equivalent to up to 26.9 million barrels of oil, plus reduced steel and cast iron use of about 42 million pounds. Adverse impacts include increased use of aluminum and plastics (5.26 million pounds each), an additional 2,200 troy ounces of platinum and palladium for larger catalytic converters, and a minor solid waste increase. Little change in air quality is anticipated because EPA emission standards will be enforced concurrently, though the lowering of the NOx standard from 3.1 to 2.3 gpm interacts with fuel economy and revised road load test procedures showed an 8 percent measured fuel economy effect.

column2: Comments were received from all domestic NPA manufacturers (AMC, Chrysler, Ford, GM, International Harvester), federal agencies (EPA, FEA, DOT, Labor, Interior, Agriculture, Forest Service, Bureau of Mines), the UAW, the Society of the Plastics Industry, Consumers Union, and others, with no comments from consumer groups in later rounds. Manufacturers generally argued the proposed level was too high, claiming fuel economy penalties of 3% to over 15% from emissions standards and revised testing procedures, and several urged separate treatment for four-wheel-drive vehicles. FEA raised concerns about market shifts from passenger automobiles to NPAs, while the National Conference of Governors' Highway Safety Representatives supported the standard as reasonable. The agency revised the EIS to reflect a range of possible standards and a two-class structure in response.
